common_name: Tibbee Crimson Clover (Mississippi-Bred Strong Fall-Growth Crimson Clover)

planting.note: Sow in fall for a winter-to-spring cover crop; Tibbee, a Mississippi State University release and companion cultivar to Bigbee berseem clover, was bred for vigorous fall and winter growth in Deep South conditions.

directions: Broadcast seed onto a prepared seedbed in fall, raking lightly to ensure good seed-to-soil contact. Tibbee was released by Mississippi State University as a companion cultivar to Bigbee berseem clover, selected for strong, rapid growth through the fall and winter months typical of Gulf South cover-cropping windows, giving it a head start on weed suppression and nitrogen fixation compared with crimson clover strains bred for more northern climates. Its brilliant crimson flower spikes in spring also provide valuable early-season forage for pollinators. Terminate at early flower stage for maximum nitrogen contribution, or allow the stand to fully flower and set seed if a self-reseeding crimson clover planting is wanted for future seasons.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Cover Crop Species Guides

common_name: Durana White Clover (Long-Persisting Heat-Tolerant White Clover)

planting.note: Sow in fall or early spring; Durana, developed at the University of Georgia, is a small-leaved white clover bred to persist far longer under heat, drought, and grazing pressure than common ladino-type white clovers.

directions: Broadcast seed onto a firm, prepared seedbed in fall or early spring, raking lightly for good seed-to-soil contact. Durana was developed at the University of Georgia specifically to address the tendency of common ladino-type white clovers to thin out and die within a season or two under Southeastern heat, drought, and grazing pressure, combining a smaller leaf size and denser stolon growth with a persistence in field trials several times longer than typical white clover strains. It works well as a living mulch and nitrogen-fixing groundcover between rows in perennial plantings, as well as in pasture and cover crop mixes. It tolerates mowing and light foot traffic well and spreads by creeping stolons to fill in bare patches over time.

common_name: AU Merit Hairy Vetch (Early-Flowering High-Biomass Hairy Vetch)

planting.note: Sow in fall for a winter-to-spring cover crop; AU Merit, bred at Auburn University, flowers roughly two weeks earlier than common hairy vetch and produces more biomass, letting it be terminated sooner ahead of a spring crop.

directions: Broadcast or drill inoculated seed into a prepared seedbed in fall, providing a companion cereal grain such as rye or wheat as a scrambling support for the vining growth if a mixed planting is wanted. AU Merit was bred at Auburn University to flower roughly two weeks earlier than common hairy vetch strains while producing greater overall biomass, letting growers terminate the cover crop and fix substantial nitrogen (often 100 lb or more per acre) sooner ahead of a spring vegetable planting than standard hairy vetch allows. Its sprawling, viny growth forms a dense, weed-suppressing mat over winter. Terminate by mowing or rolling at or just after flowering, since vetch left to set seed can become a volunteer weed in following crops.

common_name: Mt. Barker Subterranean Clover (Classic Self-Burying Reseeding Clover)

planting.note: Sow in fall for a winter annual cover crop; Mt. Barker is a classic, widely grown subterranean clover cultivar named for its unusual habit of burying its own seed pods at the soil surface after flowering, giving it excellent self-reseeding reliability.

directions: Broadcast seed onto a firm, prepared seedbed in fall, raking lightly for good seed-to-soil contact. Mt. Barker is one of the oldest and most widely grown cultivars of subterranean clover, a low-growing winter annual legume that, true to its name, buries its own developing seed pods just below the soil surface after flowering, protecting the seed and making the stand exceptionally reliable at reseeding itself year after year without replanting. Its dense, mat-forming growth suppresses winter weeds effectively and fixes nitrogen for a following crop, while its low stature makes it useful as a living mulch under fruit trees, in orchard alleys, or between vegetable rows. The plant naturally dies back in late spring as temperatures rise, leaving a nitrogen-rich mulch and buried seed ready to germinate again the following fall.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Cover Crop Species Guides
